transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

I'm really struggling with how my face looks, especially my skin. I have these awful acne scars and blemishes that make me look completely hideous, and I feel so self-conscious about it. I just don't know what to do anymore.

How much time each day do you spend thinking about these skin flaws or checking, covering, or comparing them? Do you avoid people mainly because you feel your appearance is defective, or because you fear being judged or embarrassed in social situations more generally?

I easily spend three to four hours every day obsessing over it, constantly checking mirrors, trying to cover it up with makeup, and comparing my skin to everyone I see. I avoid going out because I feel absolutely hideous and defective, rather than just being generally anxious around people.

Over the past two weeks, have you also been feeling depressed most of the day or lost interest in things you usually enjoy? If so, did those feelings start because of your skin concerns or even when you are not focused on your appearance?
I haven't really been feeling depressed or losing interest in my usual activities in general. Almost all of my distress is just completely focused on my skin concerns and how awful I look.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["Body Dysmorphic Disorder", "Major Depressive Disorder"]. Based on this conversation, Major Depressive Disorder seems unlikely because the patient denies depressed mood and loss of interest outside the appearance concern, and states the distress is specifically focused on perceived skin defects. Body Dysmorphic Disorder is strengthened by spending 3–4 hours daily obsessing about perceived flaws, repetitive mirror checking/camouflaging/comparing, and avoidance driven by feeling defective in appearance.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a preoccupation with perceived facial skin defects, spending 3–4 hours daily obsessing, mirror checking, covering with makeup, and comparing appearance to others. Avoidance is specifically due to feeling defective in appearance rather than broader social anxiety, and there is no evidence that a primary depressive syndrome better explains the distress.
